summary: Kole Jain gives six pieces of advice for beginner web designers: early designs will be bad and quantity breeds quality, there are far more usable colors than the saturated corner of the hex picker, getting hired is competitive, less is more, design does not need to be complicated, and good ideas come from gathering inspiration before starting. The design-relevant core is restraint: give a landing page one or two things to look at and click, and skip heavy 3D effects and animation when they slow loading or make navigation harder. He contrasts conversion-focused sites (an invoicing site, linear.app, huddle.works) that stay simple with an awareness site (Prometheus Fuels) where heavy scrollytelling fits its purpose. For someone building a design system, this supports defaulting to a calm, focused look and choosing how lively to be based on what the site is for, and it describes a way of working: iterate a lot, step away when stuck, and build a mood board before opening Figma [inferred].
key_ideas: Your first designs will be bad, and that is fine; design is iterative and quantity breeds quality.
When a design is not working, move on to something else and come back later instead of staring at a blank Figma page.
When he started, he kept to white, gray and one super-saturated blue and got stuck in the habit of very saturated colors; there is a whole world of other colors to explore.
Online color pickers suggest many colors; pick the one or two that catch your eye rather than using all of them.
Nature and artwork are good places to find colors you had not thought of.
Busy layouts with elements everywhere look appealing on Dribbble but hurt usability, because people get distracted easily.
You are given the whole screen but do not have to use all of it.
Big sites like Google and Apple use one call to action and one main thing in their header.
Heavy 3D effects and animations make memorable sites, but they are not worth it if they slow loading or make navigation harder.
Sites optimized for conversion can be effective with no crazy effects; heavy scrollytelling suits awareness sites that just want to be remembered.
Usability is at the heart of everything, and there is value in simplicity.
Do not jump into Figma with only a sliver of an idea; set time aside to get inspired and build a mood board first.
Judge your own resume and portfolio honestly by asking whether you would hire yourself.

rules.rule: Expect early designs to be weak and produce many iterations rather than aiming for perfection on the first attempt.
rules.why: Design is an iterative process, and quantity breeds quality.
rules.evidence: Perfection the first time round is never necessary

rules.rule: When a design is not working, move on to something else and come back to it later.
rules.why: When a design just isn't working or you feel stuck in a rut, doing something else and getting inspired lets you come back and try again.
rules.evidence: move on go try something else and then come back

rules.rule: Do not open a Figma file and stare at the page; go do something and get inspired, then come back and design.
rules.why: He says this is especially applicable when you are first learning design: doing something and getting inspired is what lets you come back and try again.
rules.evidence: don't just open a figma file and stare at the page

rules.rule: Do not limit the palette to white, gray and a single super-saturated color picked from the upper-right corner of the hex picker.
rules.why: It is fine while learning but becomes a habit that hides a whole world of other usable colors.
rules.evidence: you aren't stuck with just the upper right corner of the hex picker

rules.rule: Use an online color picker to explore palettes, and keep only the one or two suggested colors that catch your eye.
rules.why: You might not use all the colors it recommends, but it surfaces colors you would not have found yourself.
rules.evidence: online color Pickers are a great way to do this

rules.rule: Look at nature and artwork to find new colors.
rules.why: Interesting colors can be elusive even though every color is available, and these sources help rediscover them.
rules.evidence: getting inspired by looking at nature and artwork

rules.rule: On a page meant to be usable, give visitors one or maybe two things to look at and click on, and remove everything else.
rules.why: People get distracted very easily; many elements look appealing but hurt usability.
rules.evidence: don't overwhelm them give them one or maybe two things

rules.rule: Put one call to action and one main thing in the page header.
rules.why: Google and Apple do this because people get distracted very easily.
rules.evidence: they really have one call to action and one main thing in their header

rules.rule: Do not fill the whole screen with elements just because the space is available.
rules.why: Filling the screen adds aesthetic variety but reduces usability.
rules.evidence: you're given the whole screen to design something but you don't have to use it all

rules.rule: Leave out 3D effects and heavy animations when they make the website load slower or make navigation more difficult.
rules.why: Usability is at the heart of everything; such effects are memorable but not worth a slower or harder-to-navigate site.
rules.evidence: if those effects make your website load slower or make navigating more difficult

rules.rule: Do not assume a great website needs 3D animations or crazy effects; build without them unless the site calls for them.
rules.why: Not all websites need them; the invoicing site, linear.app and huddle.works are effective, aesthetic and usable with no crazy or massive 3D effects, and there is value in simplicity.
rules.evidence: it's important to remember that not all websites need that

rules.rule: Match the amount of effects to the site's goal: the simple sites shown were built for conversion, while heavy scrollytelling with animations popping in and out suits an awareness site that wants to be remembered.
rules.why: The simple sites were optimized to get people to buy something or try the product; the scrollytelling site serves a very different point (awareness) and does not need visitors to buy anything.
rules.evidence: it serves a very different point than those previous webites

rules.rule: Before starting a design, set time aside to get inspired and put together a mood board, using sites like Dribbble and Behance.
rules.why: Starting with only a sliver of an idea leads to getting stuck and frustrated; inspiration surfaces ideas you would not have had otherwise.
rules.evidence: put time aside to actually get yourself inspired to put together a mood board

rules.rule: Explore all your options instead of jumping in on the first idea you find.
rules.why: Starting from a vague idea, he would get somewhere but then get stuck because he had only a sliver of an idea, not a full one.
rules.evidence: don't get too excited and just jump in on the first thing that you find

rules.rule: Review your resume and portfolio honestly by asking whether you would hire yourself, and work on whatever makes the answer less than a definite yes.
rules.why: Getting hired is competitive and companies look at things differently from freelancers and newer designers.
rules.evidence: if I was the one hiring me would I

rules.rule: Do work you are proud of, work you would gladly show off to your friends and family.
rules.why: You do not need a university degree to get into design, so there is a lot of competition.
rules.evidence: the important thing is to do work that you're proud of

rules.rule: Ask yourself what companies are looking for and align your vision with theirs.
rules.why: Companies tend to look at things one way while freelancers and newer designers look at them differently, and moving from unstructured learning into a structured corporate environment makes it hard to portray your skills.
rules.evidence: it's important to align your visions

decisions.question: How lively should the website be: plain with no effects, a few minimal moving parts, or heavy 3D and scroll-driven animation?

options.name: No crazy effects
options.effect: Calm, fast and usable; still aesthetic and persuasive (the invoicing site shown, and linear.app with its dark mode and some glassmorphism).
options.when: Sites optimized for conversion, where people should buy or try the product.

options.name: A few minimal moving parts
options.effect: Some motion that still gets the point across without massive 3D effects (huddle.works).
options.when: When a little motion helps tell the story without slowing the site or hurting navigation [inferred].

options.name: Heavy scrollytelling and 3D
options.effect: Animations pop in and out as you scroll; very memorable, but heavy to build and render (Prometheus Fuels).
options.when: Awareness sites that want to be remembered and do not need visitors to buy anything.

decisions.recommendation: Default to simple: usability is at the heart of everything, and effects that slow loading or make navigation harder are probably not worth it. Heavy effects fit awareness sites, not conversion sites.
decisions.evidence: Design doesn't need to be complicated (4:06)

decisions.question: How many things should compete for attention in a page's header or first view?

options.name: One call to action and one main thing
options.effect: Focused and easy to act on, like the headers of Google and Apple.
options.when: Any website meant to be usable when people land on it.

options.name: One or maybe two things
options.effect: Still focused, with a second option to look at or click.
options.when: When a second action is genuinely needed [inferred].

options.name: Many elements everywhere
options.effect: Eye-catching variety that appeals to the eye but distracts people and hurts usability.
options.when: Showcase shots on Dribbble or Instagram meant to attract clicks, not usable websites.

decisions.recommendation: Give people one or maybe two things to look at and click on and get rid of everything else, because people get distracted very easily.

decisions.question: Where should palette colors come from?

options.name: White, gray and one super-saturated color
options.effect: Simple and safe, but limited to the upper-right corner of the hex picker.

options.name: Online color picker
options.effect: Surfaces many suggested colors; keep the one or two that catch your eye.
options.when: When you want to explore beyond your usual picks.

options.name: Nature and artwork
options.effect: Helps find and rediscover colors you had not thought of.

decisions.recommendation: Move beyond white, gray and very saturated colors once past the learning stage; explore with online pickers and nature and artwork.
decisions.evidence: There are more colors than you think (0:46)

caveats: The video ends with a plug for the creator's own design community (newform.community, described as 13K+ or over 13,000 designers); it is self-promotion, not advice.
Mostly personal opinion and career advice aimed at beginners, not measured findings; the conversion versus awareness split is the creator's framing.

Auto-caption errors: "dribble" is Dribbble, "figma" is Figma, "linear. apppp" is linear.app, and "take a g CPU and a half" is likely a mis-hearing of GPU; the invoicing site heard as "toah HQ" could not be identified with certainty.
The description's list of mentioned websites is truncated after coolors.co ("https://dr"), so the full list of linked sites is not available in the raw file.
Published 2024-12-02; the example websites may have changed since.
The 'getting hired' section is career advice; its rules are about the designer's own process and do not translate into design-system values.
